URL: https://www.timesofisrael.com/houthis-strike-besieged-city-in-yemen-that-un-warns-is-at-grave-risk/
(Retrieved via WebFetch; AP wire copy carried by Times of Israel, "Today, 6:01 am", by Marzouk al-Jaberi and Samy Magdy)

TAIZ, Yemen (AP) — Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a residential area in Yemen's third-largest city on Tuesday, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians in Taiz, which has been under attack and siege during the country's escalating conflict.
The Houthis have largely encircled Taiz, cutting it off from most supply routes and putting civilians at "grave risk," UN human rights chief Volker Türk said Tuesday.
The attack on Taiz came a day after a Houthi strike on a government military camp killed 73 recruits, the deadliest strike since the resurgence of the conflict over the summer, according to a senior Yemeni government official.
The conflict has intensified since forces from the internationally recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal.
Yemen has become a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
While Saudi Arabia said Tuesday that it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis, the country has struggled to defend against the rebel group's missile and drone attacks despite far superior US-supplied arms.
"Saudi Arabia is in a very difficult position," but the United States is not prepared to send troops to help, Tom Barrack, the US envoy to Syria and Iraq, told the Global Security Forum in Doha, Qatar.
Barrack said President Donald Trump "has been clear that he supports Saudi Arabia, and the backing that they need logistically we'll supply, but America getting involved in a ground kinetic battle somewhere else seems fruitless."
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the British government would expand its support to Saudi Arabia to include defensive patrols to protect Saudi cities from attacks. It means British planes would attack missiles or drones in the air, but would not strike Houthi targets on the ground. Britain had already offered to help with in-air refueling of Saudi planes.
The Egyptian government also will deploy air defense systems and aircraft to help repel missiles and drones fired toward Saudi Arabia but won't deploy ground troops to Yemen, according to a regional official who was briefed on the matter. The matter still requires parliamentary approval.
The Monday strike on the al-Alam military camp hit while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. More than 200 recruits were wounded in the attack. The recruits were all aged between 18 and 20, Shabwa governor Awad Ibn al-Wazir told AP.
